clue.text: First to support novice artist

blocks.note: a cub is a beginner, as in cub reporter
1ST, with the digit 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A beginner painter gets backing from the top dog.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'to support' means sitting underneath, so the second piece goes below the first; 1st is read with the digit as an I.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cubist is a painter of the early twentieth-century movement led by Picasso and Braque.

clue.text: Heraldic beast getting first of wizards terribly nervy

indicators.note: the opening letter of the following word is the only one taken
something done terribly is done badly, so the next word's letters end up in disorder

blocks.note: the initial of wizards
the five letters of nervy rearranged

explanation.surface: A mythical creature on a coat of arms is made jumpy by the leading sorcerer.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a two-legged winged dragon, a familiar charge in heraldry.

clue.text: Embarrassed humble character is protected by mum

indicators.note: being protected means being enclosed by a guard, so the earlier words sit inside the later one

blocks.note: Uriah Heep, the 'umble' clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield
taken as written
'mum' as in keeping quiet, so the call for silence SH

explanation.surface: A meek person, guarded by their mother, feels awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' reads as mother but means keeping quiet, as in 'mum's the word'. Uriah Heep is Dickens's falsely 'umble clerk.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheepish describes the shame-faced look of someone caught out, which is embarrassment.

clue.text: What stragglers do when inexperienced among top Scottish football clubs

indicators.note: to be among things is to be in the middle of them, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a raw recruit is untried
the Scottish Premier League, the old name for Scotland's top division

explanation.surface: Slow players straggle when green newcomers join the elite of Scottish football.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scottish Premier League (SPL) was the name of Scotland's top football division from 1998 to 2013.
explanation.definitionFit: Straggling things spread out untidily, which is to sprawl, like a straggling town or plant.

clue.text: Bandits set up in groups

indicators.note: one item placed in another is held inside it

blocks.note: bands are groups of people
to rig is to set up equipment

explanation.surface: Outlaws are organised into gangs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' looks like 'framed' or the start of a reversal, but here it is simply the wordplay for equipment being rigged.
explanation.definitionFit: Brigands are robbers who prey on travellers, the same idea as bandits.

clue.text: A power-hungry king hesitated to rewrite Sondheim musical

annotation.answer: SUNDAY IN THE PARK WITH GEORGE

indicators.note: rewriting the words means setting their letters down again in a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these words, rearranged

explanation.surface: A grasping monarch dithered over revising a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: A long anagram where the definition needs the composer's name to pin it down; the title is about the painter Seurat.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Sondheim wrote this 1984 musical about the painter Georges Seurat.

clue.text: Surrealist artist apprehending hearts as flowers

indicators.note: to apprehend is to catch and hold, so the outer name grips a letter inside it

blocks.note: Salvador Dalí, the Spanish Surrealist painter
H is the abbreviation for the card suit hearts
taken as written

explanation.surface: A painter is arrested for stealing sweethearts, who are compared to blooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' looks like a link to the definition, but it is part of the answer, tacked on at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahlias are showy garden blooms native to Mexico, so a kind of flower.

clue.text: Prime minister completely supported by the Queen, not going up to Yorkshire town

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from the bottom upwards
in a down clue, what supports something sits beneath it, so the later pieces follow

blocks.note: Lord North, British prime minister during the American War of Independence
all means wholly
Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher
taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A premier fully backed by the monarch isn't heading to a northern town.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supported by' puts later pieces underneath; Lord North led the government from 1770 to 1782.
explanation.definitionFit: Northallerton is the county town of North Yorkshire, in northern England.

clue.text: See 6
Non-flowering plant found in botanical gardens

indicators.note: something found in a phrase is sitting inside its run of letters

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A plant without blooms is growing at the botanic garden.
explanation.definitionFit: An alga is a simple water plant that reproduces without ever producing flowers.

clue.text: @Giants twittering

indicators.note: twittering is excited chatter, so the letters flutter about into a new order

blocks.note: the six letters of Giants rearranged

explanation.surface: A tweet addressed to a sports team called the Giants.
explanation.walkthrough: The '@' and 'twittering' make it read like a social-media post tagging a team; the symbol itself is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The @ character is named the at sign, used in email addresses and Twitter handles.

clue.text: Monarch possibly tracked horse at Barnet's border

indicators.note: to have tracked something is to have come along after it, so this piece follows the next

blocks.note: H is a standard abbreviation for horse
Monarch was a British carrier, so an example of a passenger air company

explanation.surface: A king may have followed a horse's trail to the edge of a London borough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tracked' means followed: the airline comes after H. Barnet is rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair), not the London borough.
explanation.definitionFit: The edge of the hair on the forehead is the hairline, so the border of one's barnet.

clue.text: Perhaps Oliver takes charge of meeting in which one's in danger of losing one's seat

definitions.text: in which one's in danger of losing one's seat

blocks.note: Oliver! is a famous stage show with songs, an example
a person who chairs a meeting presides over it

explanation.surface: Oliver runs a committee where members fear being voted out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oliver' looks like a person's name, but it is the Lionel Bart musical. The definition describes a game, rather than giving a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: In the party game, players circle chairs while music plays, and whoever is left standing when it stops is out.

clue.text: Very enthusiastic about England footballer with unknown deficiency being abandoned

indicators.note: deficient means lacking something, here a letter algebra uses for an unknown
to be about something is to go around it, so the outer word wraps the inner one

blocks.note: mad about something means keen on it
Wayne Rooney, England's former record goalscorer
x, y and z stand for unknowns in algebra

explanation.surface: A fan of an England striker is let down by his shortcomings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deficiency' signals a missing letter: the algebraic unknown is dropped from the footballer's name before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To be marooned is to be left stranded somewhere, abandoned like a castaway on an island.

clue.text: Fatter fish on stand of late

blocks.note: the chub is a freshwater fish
a bier is the stand on which a coffin rests, 'the late' being the dead

explanation.surface: Someone grows plumper on a diet of fish on the counter recently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of late' seems to mean 'recently', but here it means 'for the late', i.e. the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Chubby means plump, so its comparative chubbier means fatter.

clue.text: Comic book character might be Female, cryptically

indicators.note: this warns that the word must be split and each part read as a coded abbreviation or synonym

blocks.note: split as FE + MALE: FE is the chemical symbol for iron, and male means man

explanation.surface: A superhero might turn out to be a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Female' as FE-MALE, and translate each half.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron Man is the Marvel superhero Tony Stark, who wears a powered armour suit.

clue.text: Sort of cinema seat that engulfs you

indicators.note: to engulf is to swallow up completely, so one word closes around the other

blocks.note: a crude British word for the backside, which one sits on
the old form of you

explanation.surface: A cinema chair so deep it swallows you up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' means the backside, not a chair, using a crude British word; 'you' gives its archaic form.
explanation.definitionFit: An art house cinema screens independent and foreign films rather than mainstream releases.

clue.text: Sleuth involved in confidence trick

indicators.note: something involved is tangled up, so the letters become knotted into a new order

blocks.note: the six letters of Sleuth rearranged

explanation.surface: A detective gets mixed up in a con.
explanation.definitionFit: A hustle is a swindle or scam, the same as a confidence trick.

clue.text: Good start for game

blocks.note: G is the usual abbreviation for good
to start or rouse a bird is to flush it from cover

explanation.surface: A promising opening to a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a sporting contest but means wild birds shot for sport; 'start' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: Grouse are moorland birds shot in season, a classic example of game in Britain.

clue.text: Pleasant-sounding rock

indicators.note: sounding tells you to go by what the word sounds like when spoken

blocks.note: nice is a synonym for pleasant

explanation.surface: A rock that makes an agreeable noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The G of the answer is silent, so it is said just like the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Gneiss is a banded metamorphic stone formed under heat and pressure.

clue.text: Mother unfortunately got up a salutation

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: an informal word for mother
an exclamation of regret

explanation.surface: Sadly Mum stood up to give a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Salaam is a greeting used in Muslim countries, often with a low bow.

clue.text: Computer tycoon no longer providing employment

blocks.note: first meaning: Steve ..., the late co-founder of Apple
second meaning: positions of paid work

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tech boss who has stopped hiring; 'no longer' means he has died.
explanation.definitionFit: Steve Jobs died in 2011, and jobs are posts or positions of paid work.

clue.text: Is it used to make goat's cheese?

definitions.text: Is it used to make goat's cheese?

blocks.clueFragment: Is it used to make goat's cheese?
blocks.note: surface reading: an ingredient in a dairy product made from goat's milk
setter's reading: a goat is an animal that butts, so the drink is the milk of one that butts

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a question about cheesemaking, but a goat is an animal that butts, so it is a 'butter', and its milk is the dairy drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the sour liquid left after churning cream, also used in baking and cheesemaking.

clue.text: May Stallone nude performance be making of Lloyd Webber musical

indicators.note: a performance puts on a show, so the letters are acted out in a new arrangement

blocks.note: the fifteen letters of these three words rearranged

explanation.surface: A cheeky stage appearance by Sylvester Stallone without clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Lloyd Webber wrote this one-woman song cycle with Don Black, first staged in 1979.
